title: The HPA Axis in Trauma
subtitle: Cortisol regulation under acute and prolonged threat
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating the hpa axis in trauma across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain the hpa axis in trauma in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in the hpa axis in trauma.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to the hpa axis in trauma.

sections.explainSimply: The HPA axis coordinates a slower hormonal stress response and helps mobilise energy.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Trauma-related disorders may show altered cortisol timing, reactivity or feedback, but direction and magnitude vary across samples, sex, development and chronicity.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: CRH, ACTH and cortisol operate through feedback loops involving hypothalamus, pituitary, adrenal cortex, hippocampus and prefrontal regions.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of the hpa axis in trauma as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need the hpa axis in trauma to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Single cortisol measurements do not diagnose PTSD or treatment need.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use the hpa axis in trauma to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses the hpa axis in trauma to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Single cortisol measurements do not diagnose PTSD or treatment need. Evidence classification: established physiology; mixed disorder-specific patterns.
